blocks.text: If you've ever wondered who the aerobics instructor in Eric Prydz's "Call On Me" film clip actually was - and whether you can take her class here in Bondi - here's the short answer. Her name is Deanne Berry, she's a Sydney-born professional dancer, and after that leotard-and-legwarmers routine made her one of the most recognised faces on British TV, she came home to Australia and has taught high-energy dance-fitness right here on the beach. I went looking for her story, because a local link to one of the 2000s' most talked-about music videos is far too good to keep quiet.

blocks.text: The most talked-about aerobics video of the 2000s

You almost certainly remember it: a room full of dancers in high-cut leotards, legwarmers and sweatbands, working through a suggestive aerobics routine to Eric Prydz's thumping club track. Released in 2004 on Ministry of Sound, and built around a sampled vocal from Steve Winwood's "Valerie", the song became a UK number-one hit and the video one of the most recognised - and most debated - dance clips of the decade. At the time it was about as risqué as a mainstream music video got. And the instructor front and centre? A Bondi local in the making.

As Deanne tells it, her career began in Sydney at 16, dancing and performing before touring interstate and through Asia with musicals and artists. That work eventually took her to the UK, where a tour backing Sir Cliff Richard led to a stint in London - and, during a break between concert dates, to a casting call for an eighties-inspired Ministry of Sound video. She landed the role of the instructor, and a few days later found herself in that now-infamous black thong leotard, legwarmers and not much else.

She didn't expect it to go anywhere. "I thought not too many people would see it," she told me - so jumping around and pelvic-thrusting felt harmless enough. Then the track shot to the top of the charts, the video spread around the world, and almost overnight she went from working dancer to accidental fitness guru. She took the moment and ran with it: enrolling in fitness courses, choreographing and presenting a Ministry of Sound fitness DVD that sold strongly, and later waking up Britain as a fitness presenter on breakfast television.

Back in Australia, Deanne has channelled all of that into a dance-conditioning class - each workout themed to a different pop artist, so you sweat your way through the sounds of the likes of Rihanna, Kylie, Beyoncé and Michael Jackson while building stamina, flexibility and strength. Her pitch is simple: leave your inhibitions at the door, come with an open mind, and don't worry if you can't dance. She's had mums and daughters in the same session; the only real requirement is a love of moving to music.

blocks.title: Classes and studios change - check before you go
blocks.text: This interview dates back a few years, and dance-fitness timetables and studios move around. Rather than turn up on spec, look up Deanne Berry's current classes and locations on her own website and social channels for what's actually running now.

Fancy recreating the routine? Deanne told me she still gets asked to bring back the "Call On Me" moves at parties and events, and clearly still loves performing the track - so if you're planning an eighties-themed do, she's the person who danced the original.

items.q: Who was the aerobics instructor in the Call On Me video?
items.a: Deanne Berry, a Sydney-born professional dancer. She was cast as the instructor for Eric Prydz's 2004 "Call On Me" clip and later returned to Australia, where she has taught dance-fitness in the Bondi area.

items.q: Is the Call On Me clip really by Eric Prydz?
items.a: Yes. "Call On Me" was released by Swedish producer Eric Prydz in 2004 on Ministry of Sound and built around a sampled vocal from Steve Winwood's "Valerie". It became a UK number-one hit.

items.q: Can I take Deanne Berry's class in Bondi?
items.a: She has run dance-fitness classes in the Bondi area, but timetables and studios change over time. Check her current website and social channels for what's on now rather than relying on this older interview.

items.q: Do I need dance experience to join?
items.a: No. Her classes are pitched at all levels - she's had complete beginners, and even mums and daughters, in the same session. The only thing you really need is a willingness to move to music.

items.q: Did the Call On Me video top the charts?
items.a: Yes - the track was a UK number-one hit and the video became one of the most recognised and talked-about dance clips of the 2000s.

blocks.text: It's a lovely little piece of Bondi trivia: the face of one of the era's most famous music videos quietly getting people dancing a few streets back from the sand. If the story's tempted you to try a class, do check what she's running before you go - and either way, next time that Eric Prydz track comes on, you'll know the instructor is one of our own.
